## The brief is deliberately too large

```{=html}
<div class="stage opening-stage">
  <div>
    <div class="eyebrow">THE WORKED EXAMPLE</div>
    <p class="big-claim">Build a native, cross-platform image editor with Photoshop-scale breadth.</p>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>~540k</b><span>lines of Rust</span></div>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>25</b><span>library crates</span></div>
    <div class="metric-line"><b>8,000+</b><span>tests</span></div>
  </div>
  <figure class="hero-frame"><img src="images/photocraft-demo.jpg" alt="PhotoCraft editing Hokusai's Great Wave with adjustment and layer panels visible"><figcaption>PhotoCraft, in the middle of real work</figcaption></figure>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
PhotoCraft is a useful test because the brief is unreasonable for one person or one agent.  A serious image editor needs a document model, PSD fidelity, color management, painting, text, vectors, GPU rendering, automation, platform packaging, and a large, familiar UI.

The interesting result is not that agents can type half a million lines.  It is that the repository can absorb parallel work without turning those lines into an unmaintainable pile.

The figures on the slide are counted from the current source and architecture document.  Sources: [architecture](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/architecture.md), [workspace manifest](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/Cargo.toml).
:::

## `AGENTS.md` is the control plane

```{=html}
<div class="stage document-stage">
  <div class="artifact paper">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>AGENTS.md</span><span>read first</span></div>
    <h3>One shared operating manual</h3>
    <div class="rule"><b>Orient</b><span>Architecture, roadmap, gaps, scorecard</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Choose</b><span>Highest-ranked work that nobody owns</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Build</b><span>One command, one module, one testable slice</span></div>
    <div class="rule"><b>Finish</b><span>Run the gates and leave a terse dev log</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy">
    <p class="big-claim compact">The prompt is part of the codebase.</p>
    <p>Every worker starts with the same map, rules, and definition of done.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">Less private context.  Fewer invented conventions.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The first artifact is the most important one.  `AGENTS.md` is not a welcome note.  It is the operating system for contributors and agents.

It tells a worker what to read, how to pick work, what must never happen, which files are shared, how to validate a change, and how to leave the repository for the next worker.  That turns tacit maintainer knowledge into versioned project state.

It is deliberately specific.  “Everything is a command,” “never panic on input,” and “new behavior goes in a new module” are stronger than general advice about writing good code.  Source: [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/AGENTS.md).
:::

## The architecture is a map of safe ownership

```{=html}
<div class="architecture-stage">
  <div class="layer-stack">
    <div class="layer l6"><b>L6</b><span>UI · automation</span></div>
    <div class="layer l5"><b>L5</b><span>engine · command registry</span></div>
    <div class="layer l4"><b>L4</b><span>I/O · sandboxed plug-ins</span></div>
    <div class="layer l3"><b>L3</b><span>CPU/GPU composition · native format</span></div>
    <div class="layer l2"><b>L2</b><span>paint · text · vector · algorithms</span></div>
    <div class="layer l1"><b>L1</b><span>document model</span></div>
    <div class="layer l0"><b>L0</b><span>geometry · color · raster · codecs</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="side-copy architecture-copy">
    <div class="eyebrow">ARTIFACT · docs/architecture.md</div>
    <p class="big-claim compact">A crate may only depend downward.</p>
    <p><code>cargo xtask layers</code> checks the rule.  The diagram is not a suggestion.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">An agent can own a layer without learning the whole application.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Parallel work needs boundaries that a machine can enforce.  PhotoCraft has explicit crate layers.  Foundation code sits at the bottom, then the document model, algorithms, composition, I/O, engine, and finally UI and automation.

The `xtask layers` command checks that dependencies only point downward.  An agent working on a codec cannot quietly pull UI types into the format layer.  The architectural map therefore doubles as a map of safe ownership.

Sources: [architecture](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/architecture.md), [layer checker](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/xtask/src/layers.rs).
:::

## The menu is a contract

```{=html}
<div class="stage menu-stage">
  <div class="artifact code-paper">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>menu_catalog.rs</span><span>631 items</span></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>File › Export</span><b>Export As…</b><code>file.export.exportAs</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Edit › Transform</span><b>Warp</b><code>edit.transform.warp</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Layer › New</span><b>Layer…</b><code>layer.new.layer</code></div>
    <div class="menu-row"><span>Filter › Blur</span><b>Gaussian Blur…</b><code>filter.blur.gaussianBlur</code></div>
  </div>
  <div class="menu-result">
    <div class="ring"><span>631</span><small>of 631 live</small></div>
    <p>Matching command ID found: enabled.<br>Missing implementation: visible, but disabled.</p>
    <p class="accent-note">The surface area becomes a measurable backlog.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The menu catalog is a surprisingly powerful planning artifact.  It records the whole target menu structure with a stable command ID for every item.

When the engine registers that ID, the menu item becomes live automatically.  The agent implementing Gaussian Blur does not also need to understand menu construction, shortcuts, automation, and parity reporting.  One identifier joins those systems.

The generated parity document currently reports 631 of 631 menu items live, and a test prevents the floor from falling.  That is breadth, not proof of full behavioral depth, which matters later.  Sources: [menu catalog](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/crates/ui-egui/src/menu_catalog.rs), [parity floor](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/crates/ui-egui/src/parity.rs), [generated parity report](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/parity-checklist.md).
:::

## Everything becomes one command

```{=html}
<div class="command-stage">
  <div class="artifact command-spec">
    <div class="artifact-bar"><span>CommandSpec</span><span>the engine seam</span></div>
    <pre><code>id        "filter.blur.gaussianBlur"
label     "Gaussian Blur…"
menu      ["Filter", "Blur"]
params    { radius: 0..1000 }
enabled   has_pixel_layer
run       gaussian_blur</code></pre>
  </div>
  <div class="clients">
    <div><b>Desktop</b><span>menu click</span></div>
    <div><b>CLI</b><span>headless run</span></div>
    <div><b>MCP</b><span>agent tool</span></div>
    <div><b>Actions</b><span>record + replay</span></div>
  </div>
  <p class="command-caption">Four clients.  One behavior.  One undo step.</p>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
“Everything is a command” is the central design choice.  A command carries its stable ID, label, menu path, shortcut, parameter description, precondition, implementation, and whether it belongs in the journal.

The desktop UI, CLI, MCP server, control channel, recorded actions, and plug-ins all converge on the same registry.  That removes duplicate behavior and gives agents a structured way to discover what exists.

A UI gesture ends in a command too.  The command owns the edit and therefore the undo boundary.  Source: [command registry](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/crates/engine/src/commands.rs).
:::

## The backlog is executable

```{=html}
<div class="tracking-stage">
  <div class="tracking-doc road"><span>ROADMAP.md</span><b>What matters now?</b><small>stage · milestones · honest readiness</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc gaps"><span>docs/gaps.md</span><b>What should an agent pick?</b><small>G1–G17 · ranked by user impact</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc score"><span>scorecard/*.toml</span><b>What counts as done?</b><small>status · issue · evidence · budget</small></div>
  <div class="tracking-doc report"><span>docs/scorecard.md</span><b>Does the report match reality?</b><small>generated · checked in CI</small></div>
</div>
<p class="tracking-caption">Strategy becomes a queue.  The queue becomes evidence.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The work queue is also kept in the repository.  `ROADMAP.md` says where the product is.  `docs/gaps.md` ranks the known shortfalls.  The scorecard sources attach a status, issue, and code evidence to individual capabilities and performance budgets.

An agent can choose useful work without a meeting.  More importantly, it can update the same artifact when the change lands.  CI regenerates the scorecard and fails if the report is stale.

This is how the swarm avoids optimizing for whatever task happens to be easiest to prompt.  Sources: [roadmap](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/ROADMAP.md), [ranked gaps](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/gaps.md), [scorecard](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/scorecard.md).
:::

## The repository runs the swarm

```{=html}
<div class="swarm-stage">
  <div class="agent-field" aria-label="Several independent agents working around a shared repository">
    <span class="agent a1">A</span><span class="agent a2">A</span><span class="agent a3">A</span><span class="agent a4">A</span>
    <span class="agent a5">A</span><span class="agent a6">A</span><span class="agent a7">A</span><span class="agent a8">A</span>
    <div class="repo-core"><img src="images/photocraft-mark.png" alt="PhotoCraft application mark"><b>REPO</b><small>rules · queue · evidence</small></div>
  </div>
  <div class="swarm-rules">
    <div><b>Separate build directories</b><span>No Cargo lock queue</span></div>
    <div><b>Explicit file ownership</b><span>Small edits to shared registries</span></div>
    <div><b>New command modules</b><span>Parallel additions rarely collide</span></div>
    <div><b>Green handoffs</b><span>The next worker starts from a stable tree</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
There is no magical conductor in the middle.  The repository coordinates the swarm.

Agents use separate build directories, own narrow file sets, add behavior in new command modules, and keep edits to shared registries small.  The shared artifacts tell each worker what matters and what “finished” means.

This is closer to a well-designed distributed system than a group chat.  Workers do not need to know everything the others know.  They need stable contracts and low-conflict places to write.  Source: [parallel-agent rules](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/AGENTS.md#6-parallel-agents).
:::

## Vertical slices keep merges boring

```{=html}
<div class="slice-stage">
  <div class="slice-list">
    <div><i>01</i><b>Choose one visible gap</b><span>“Add Gaussian Blur”</span></div>
    <div><i>02</i><b>Add one command module</b><span><code>gaussian_blur_cmds.rs</code></span></div>
    <div><i>03</i><b>Reuse the lower layer</b><span><code>algo::blur::gaussian</code></span></div>
    <div><i>04</i><b>Prove failure and success</b><span>bad params · pixels · undo</span></div>
    <div><i>05</i><b>Raise the evidence</b><span>parity · scorecard · dev log</span></div>
  </div>
  <figure class="slice-image"><img src="images/photocraft-filters.jpg" alt="PhotoCraft applying a Twirl filter to The Starry Night"><figcaption>A complete user-visible slice</figcaption></figure>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The unit of parallel work is a vertical slice, not an abstract layer.  A useful slice starts with a visible gap, adds one command, reuses or extends a lower-level algorithm, proves both success and graceful failure, and updates the evidence.

That shape is easy to review and easy to merge.  It avoids the classic swarm failure where one agent builds a framework, another builds a UI, and neither quite matches the other.

The shared command registry still needs a small edit, but the implementation stays in a new module.  Source: [contributor checklist](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/contributing.md), [agent rules](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/AGENTS.md).
:::

## Photoshop becomes a test oracle

```{=html}
<div class="oracle-stage">
  <div class="oracle-image">
    <img src="images/photocraft-adjustments.jpg" alt="PhotoCraft displaying Monet's Impression, Sunrise with Levels and Histogram panels">
    <div class="pixel-chip">difference ≤ 2 / 255</div>
  </div>
  <div class="oracle-copy">
    <div class="eyebrow">ARTIFACT · TEST CORPUS</div>
    <p class="big-claim compact">The target application supplies the expected pixels.</p>
    <ol>
      <li>Build a document in Photoshop</li>
      <li>Keep its flattened compatibility image</li>
      <li>Render it with PhotoCraft's CPU compositor</li>
      <li>Compare, then raise a floor that cannot fall</li>
    </ol>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Natural-language acceptance criteria are not enough for compositing.  PhotoCraft uses Photoshop-authored PSD files as test oracles.

The files contain Photoshop's flattened compatibility image.  PhotoCraft renders the document through its CPU compositor and compares the pixels, normally allowing at most two levels of difference out of 255.  The GPU compositor is then checked against the CPU reference.

Pass counts have floors.  When a fix raises one, later changes are not allowed to lower it.  The target product has been turned into durable evidence instead of a vague visual reference.  Sources: [corpus rules](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/AGENTS.md), [I/O corpus tests](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/crates/io/tests/corpus.rs).
:::

## Agents can operate the product

```{=html}
<div class="operate-stage">
  <div class="operate-code"><div class="artifact-bar"><span>MCP / control protocol</span><span>same command IDs</span></div><pre><code>command_list  { filter: "blur" }
command_run   { id, params }
doc_inspect   { layers, history }
render_preview{ max_side: 1024 }
ui_screenshot { live window }</code></pre></div>
  <div class="observe-loop">
    <div><b>Inspect</b><span>state, commands, preconditions</span></div>
    <div><b>Act</b><span>the same engine path as the UI</span></div>
    <div><b>See</b><span>bounded render or full screenshot</span></div>
    <div><b>Correct</b><span>use the returned error, not a guess</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="operate-caption">A bug report can be a runnable script.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
Agents are not restricted to editing source and hoping.  They can operate the product headlessly through the CLI and MCP, or drive the live desktop app through the control channel.

The tools expose the command catalog, current preconditions, document state, rendered previews, UI state, pointer input, and screenshots.  The file authority is capability-scoped rather than ambient.

That creates a closed loop: inspect, act, see, correct.  It also makes a bug report executable.  The reproduction can be a short sequence of commands rather than a paragraph describing where somebody clicked.  Sources: [MCP conventions](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/mcp.md), [control protocol](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/control-protocol.md).
:::

## Why Rust fits this system

```{=html}
<div class="rust-stage">
  <div class="rust-word">Rust</div>
  <div class="rust-reasons">
    <div><b>One language</b><span>engine, native UI, CLI, plug-in host, web build</span></div>
    <div><b>Explicit boundaries</b><span>types make command and crate seams harder to blur</span></div>
    <div><b>Native performance</b><span>rayon on the CPU, wgpu on the GPU</span></div>
    <div><b>Portable core</b><span>macOS · Windows · Linux · FreeBSD · WebAssembly</span></div>
    <div><b>Constrained danger</b><span><code>unsafe_code = "forbid"</code> across the workspace</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Rust is not just a speed choice here.  It lets the project keep the engine, native interface, command-line tools, automation server, and browser build in one language and one type system.

The ownership model and explicit error types support the project's “never crash on input” rule.  They do not make correctness automatic, but they make hidden sharing and unchecked failure harder to introduce across agent boundaries.

Performance work remains direct: Rayon handles CPU-parallel tiles and wgpu handles the GPU.  The same core compiles to WebAssembly.  The workspace forbids unsafe code, with one isolated tablet-input exception documented in the agent guide.  Sources: [workspace manifest](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/Cargo.toml), [architecture](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/architecture.md), [development guide](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/development.md).
:::

## Quality is enforced at the borders

```{=html}
<div class="gates-stage">
  <div class="gate"><span>FORMAT</span><b>rustfmt</b><small>one mechanical style</small></div>
  <div class="gate"><span>SAFETY</span><b>clippy</b><small>panics and shortcuts denied</small></div>
  <div class="gate"><span>BEHAVIOR</span><b>8,000+ tests</b><small>unit · corpus · regression</small></div>
  <div class="gate"><span>STRUCTURE</span><b>layers</b><small>dependencies point down</small></div>
  <div class="gate"><span>PORTABILITY</span><b>wasm</b><small>web-safe core stays web-safe</small></div>
  <div class="gate"><span>TRUTH</span><b>scorecard</b><small>generated evidence stays current</small></div>
</div>
<p class="gate-caption">Agents are allowed to be fast because the borders are strict.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
The system expects agents to make mistakes.  Quality comes from gates at the borders, not from assuming every worker has perfect judgment.

Formatting removes stylistic debate.  Clippy denies dangerous shortcuts.  Tests cover local behavior and real files.  The layer checker preserves architecture.  The Wasm build catches accidental platform coupling.  The generated scorecard catches stale claims.

The full gate is expensive, so agents run narrow checks while iterating and the complete relevant set before finishing.  Sources: [CI workflow](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/.github/workflows/ci.yml), [development guide](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/development.md).
:::

## Fast does not mean finished

```{=html}
<div class="honesty-stage">
  <figure><img src="images/photocraft-vector.jpg" alt="PhotoCraft editing vector shapes over Monet's Water Lilies"><figcaption>Wide, convincing feature coverage</figcaption></figure>
  <div class="honesty-copy">
    <div class="paired-stat"><b>100%</b><span>menu breadth<br><small>631 / 631 live</small></span></div>
    <div class="paired-stat warning"><b>~45%</b><span>ready for real work<br><small>project estimate</small></span></div>
    <div class="paired-stat warning"><b>3 / 56</b><span>performance scenarios within budget<br><small>measured scorecard</small></span></div>
    <p>The system records the gap between a feature existing and a feature being dependable.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
This slide is important because swarm speed can create a convincing surface before the depth is ready.

The menu is completely live, yet the project's own roadmap estimates readiness for real work at roughly 45 percent.  The scorecard records only 3 of 56 performance scenarios within budget in its current baseline, with many missing, unmeasured, or over budget.

The honest numbers are a feature of the system.  They stop broad coverage from being mistaken for a finished product and give the next wave of agents something concrete to improve.  Sources: [roadmap](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/ROADMAP.md), [scorecard](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft/blob/c699e3cda69f4852b43c0b191ab0091aaeff9d6a/docs/scorecard.md).
:::

## A reusable swarm recipe {.final-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="recipe">
  <div><i>01</i><b>Write the operating manual</b><span>Put judgment, constraints, and finish criteria in the repository.</span></div>
  <div><i>02</i><b>Turn the product into stable contracts</b><span>Commands, schemas, crate seams, and file ownership.</span></div>
  <div><i>03</i><b>Turn ambition into a ranked queue</b><span>Roadmap, gaps, budgets, and evidence.</span></div>
  <div><i>04</i><b>Give workers a closed loop</b><span>Inspect, act, observe, test, and recover without a human relay.</span></div>
  <div><i>05</i><b>Make truth harder to fake</b><span>Generated reports, regression floors, oracles, and honest gaps.</span></div>
</div>
<p class="final-thought">The swarm scales when the work is legible.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
PhotoCraft's recipe transfers well beyond image editing.

Start with an operating manual that contains real project judgment.  Define stable contracts that create low-conflict ownership.  Convert the product vision into a ranked queue with measurable evidence.  Give workers the tools to operate and observe the system themselves.  Finally, make the truth difficult to fake with generated reports, floors, and external oracles.

The reusable idea is simple: the swarm scales when the work is legible.  Agents do not need a larger prompt.  They need a repository that can explain itself, constrain change, and verify the result.
:::
